deep.reconstruction:
PROBLEM. Gauss is finding all complex roots of trinomial equations x^7 - 3x^2 + A = 0 for a sequence of values of A, using 7-place logarithm-sine tables. He headed this sequence 'Es folgt die dritte Parallele' ('The third parallel follows'). The left columns finish the previous page's equation; the right part starts a new family of four equations: A = 0, 4, 2-2i and (next page) 2-sqrt2-sqrt2*i.

METHOD (implicit steps mine). Write x = r e^{i phi} and A = c e^{iC}. Then x^7 + A = 3x^2, so the vectors x^7, A and 3x^2 form a triangle. Projecting onto suitable directions (the sine rule) gives:
(1) r^7 sin(5phi) = c sin(2phi - C)
(2) 3 r^2 sin(5phi) = c sin(7phi - C)
Eliminating r via r^14 = (r^7)^2 = (r^2)^7 gives one real equation in phi:
F(phi) = 7 log|sin(7phi-C)| - 2 log|sin(2phi-C)| - 5 log|sin(5phi)| = log(1/lambda),
where 1/lambda = 3^7/c^5. In the notation of the previous page, b^7 = 3^7 has log 3.3398488.

For a trial phi (in whole seconds) Gauss:
- forms the three angles 2phi-C, 5phi and 7phi-C;
- looks up log sin of each, with its tabular change per 1 arc-second (21.055*cot);
- multiplies the logs by 2, 5 and 7, and the changes by 4, 25 and 49 (chain rule);
- applies one linear (regula-falsi/Newton) correction to hit log(1/lambda).
He then takes log r = [log|sin(2phi-C)| - log|sin 5phi| + log c]/7. When the sine ratio is negative he marks log r with 'n'; this means r<0, i.e. the root lies at phi+180 deg. Finally Re x = r cos phi and Im x = r sin phi are obtained by adding log cos and log sin.

LEFT COLUMNS. Equation of p.224: x^7 - 3x^2 + 3.6686463 - 1.6686463i = 0. Here log c = 0.6053378, C = 335 deg 32'31.464", and log(1/lambda) = 3.3398488 - 3.0266890 = 0.3131598.
(a) phi = 103 deg 41'58". Angles 231 deg 51'24.536", 158 deg 29'50", 30 deg 21'14.536". F = 0.3130872 with slope +3033 per second. Correction 726/3033 = 0.239", giving phi = 103 deg 41'58.239". log r^7 = 0.3315603 + 0.6053378 = 0.9368981 and log r = 0.1338426, marked n. Root x = +0.3223139 - 1.3222338i.
(b) phi = 134 deg 5'12". Angles 292 deg 37'52.536", 310 deg 26'0", 243 deg 3'52.536". F = 0.3131232 with slope 1011, so phi = 134 deg 5'12.362". log r = 0.0984380. Root x = -0.8727488 + 0.9010232i.
(c) phi = 158 deg 3'9". F = 0.3131774 with slope 893.7, so phi = 158 deg 3'8.803". log r = 0.0219689, marked n. Root x = +0.9756524 - 0.3931507i.
(d) phi = 172 deg 33'39". F = 0.3131303 with slope -1773.6, so phi = 172 deg 33'38.834". log r = 0.0064435. Root x = -1.0064042 + 0.1314096i.
Together with the roots of p.224 (+0.4089901+1.3225680i and +1.1665145+0.2552124i), these give six roots. The seventh, -0.9943177 - 0.8948292i, appears on p.224 and was evidently obtained from sum of roots = 0. My sum of the six roots gives -0.9943179 - 0.8948287i.

RIGHT: FIRST EQUATION, x^7 - 3x^2 = 0. Roots x = 0 (double) and the fifth roots of 3. log 3^{1/5} = 0.0954243, so r = 1.24573. The table gives:
- 72 deg: log cos 9.48998, log sin 9.97821, so x = 0.38494 + 1.18475i;
- 144 deg: log cos 9.90796n, log sin 9.76922, so x = -1.00782 + 0.73222i.
The conjugates are implicit.

SECOND EQUATION, x^7 - 3x^2 + 4 = 0. f^5 = 4^5 has log 3.0103000, and log(1/lambda) = 3.3398488 - 3.0103000 = 0.3295488. C = 0.
- Trial phi = 16 deg 6'32": angles 32 deg 13'4", 80 deg 32'40", 112 deg 45'44".
- F = 0.3295318 with slope -652.3 per second. Correction -170/652.3 = -0.261", giving phi = 16 deg 6'31.739".
- log(sin2phi/sin5phi) = 9.7327814 with slope 49.3 (margin: 66.8, 17.5), corrected to 9.7327801.
- Adding log 4 = 0.6020600 gives log r^7 = 0.3348401, so log r = 0.0478343.
- Root x = 1.0726020 + 0.3097694i.

THIRD EQUATION, x^7 - 3x^2 + 2 - 2i = 0. C = 315 deg and log c = log(2 sqrt2) = 0.4515450. log c^5 = 2.2577250, so log(1/lambda) = 1.0821238.
- Trial phi = 7 deg 48'5": angles 2phi-C = 60 deg 36'10", 5phi = 39 deg 0'25", 7phi-C = 99 deg 36'35".
- log sines 9.9401366 (+11.8), 9.7989368 (+26.0), 9.9938627 (-3.6).
- 2x, 5x, 7x: 9.8802732 (+47.2), 8.9946840 (+650.0), 9.9570389 (-176.4). Denominator 8.8749572 (+697.2).
- F = 1.0820817 with slope -873.6. Correction -421/873.6 = -0.482", giving phi = 7 deg 48'4.518".
- log ratio 0.1411998 (slope -106.4), corrected by +51 to 0.1412049. Adding 0.4515450 gives 0.5927499, so log r = 0.0846786.
- log cos phi = 9.9959618 and log sin phi = 9.1326991, so x = 1.2040385 + 0.1649597i.
The next page continues with the other roots of this equation and then with A = 2-sqrt2-sqrt2*i.

The four A-values of this 'Parallele' (0, 4, 2-2i, 2-sqrt2-sqrt2 i) all lie on the circle |A-2| = 2. Gauss seems to be following the roots as A runs along a path. The exact meaning of 'Parallele' is not clear to me.
errors: No substantive errors found; all checked log-sine values, multiples, tabular differences and interpolations agree to about 1 unit in the 7th decimal.

First equation: 10^0.0954243 = 1.245731, so the real root/modulus should be 1.24573. The page appears to read 1,24571; this is a last-digit slip or a misreading. The derived 5-figure values 0.38494/0.38495 and 1.18475/1.18476 are consistent to 5-place-log accuracy.
Left column (a): the correction 726/3033 = 0.2394" implies 103 deg 41'58.239"; the transcription's 58,249 is probably a misreading (see corrections).

The 'n' on log r (e.g. 0,1338426n and 0,0219689n) is not an error: it records that sin(2phi-C)/sin(5phi) < 0. The root then lies at phi+180 deg, and the signs of the final real and imaginary parts are correctly flipped.

results.what: Computation of complex roots of the trinomial x^7 - 3x^2 + A = 0. Polar substitution gives the triangle/sine-rule relations r^7 sin5phi = c sin(2phi-C) and 3r^2 sin5phi = c sin(7phi-C). Eliminating r leaves a single equation in the argument phi, solved with log-sine tables and linear interpolation using tabular differences.
results.modern_name: Trigonometric/logarithmic solution of trinomial equations (Gauss's method for x^{m+n}+e x^m+f=0); in effect Newton/regula-falsi on a real equation for the argument
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, 'Beitraege zur Theorie der algebraischen Gleichungen' (1849/50), second part on trinomial equations

results.what: Determining the last (seventh) root from the vanishing coefficient of x^6, i.e. sum of roots = 0; also used as a check (carried out on p.224).
results.modern_name: Vieta's relation used as a closing check

results.what: Systematic computation of roots for a family of constants A (0, 4, 2-2i, 2-sqrt2-sqrt2 i, all on |A-2|=2) under the heading 'dritte Parallele'. This apparently tracks how the roots move as A varies.
results.modern_name: Numerical continuation / root-locus tracking of polynomial roots in a parameter
results.usually_credited_to: unsure (root-locus ideas are 20th-century; continuation of roots is implicit in 19th-century work on algebraic functions)

deep.surprise_reason: The method is exactly the logarithmic-trigonometric treatment of trinomial equations that Gauss himself published in 1849/50, so the page is a worked numerical example of a known Gauss technique. The only mildly notable aspect is the organized sweep over parameter values on a circle ('Parallele'). This suggests an experimental study of root motion connected with his work on the fundamental theorem, but it is not a new result.
